working: \(y = e^{x}(A\cos x + B\sin x)\) is the general solution of a linear ODE with roots \(1 \pm i\), i.e. \((D-1)^2 + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow D^2 - 2D + 2 = 0\), so \(y'' - 2y' + 2y = 0\), i.e. \(y'' = 2y' - 2y\). Numeric check with \(A=1, B=0\): \(y = e^x\cos x\), \(y' = e^x(\cos x - \sin x)\), \(y'' = -2e^x\sin x\); then \(2y' - 2y = -2e^x\sin x = y''\).

subtopic: Heights and Distances from Angles of Elevation
working: Observer's eye is at height 30 m, the same level as the flag top; let \(d\) be the horizontal distance. Depression angles: to the flag foot (building top, 25 m) \(\alpha\) with \(\tan\alpha = 5/d\); to the building foot (0 m) \(\beta\) with \(\tan\beta = 30/d\). Flag subtends \(\alpha\), building subtends \(\beta - \alpha\); equating gives \(\beta = 2\alpha\). So \(30/d = \frac{2(5/d)}{1 - 25/d^2} = \frac{10d}{d^2-25}\), hence \(30(d^2-25) = 10d^2 \Rightarrow 20d^2 = 750 \Rightarrow d^2 = 37.5 = 75/2\), \(d = 5\sqrt{3/2}\). Because the flag top is level with the observer, the distance to it equals \(d\). Check: \(d = 6.1237\), \(\alpha = \arctan(0.8165) = 39.232^\circ\), \(\beta = \arctan(4.899) = 78.463^\circ = 2\alpha\) ✓.

working: A diagonal matrix has every off-diagonal entry zero. The entry \(b\) sits in position (3,2), which is off the diagonal, so \(b = 0\).

Write \(v = (p,q,r)^T\); then \(B = vv^T\) and \(A\) is the skew-symmetric cross-product matrix for \(v\), so \(Av = v \times v = 0\). Hence \(AB = (Av)v^T = 0\), the null matrix. Verified numerically with \(p=2, q=-3, r=5\): every entry of AB is 0.

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), induction gives \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix}1&na\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^4 = \begin{bmatrix}1&4a\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Checked numerically with \(a=7\): \(A^4 = \begin{bmatrix}1&28\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(28 = 4\times 7\).
Multiplying every element of A by 3 is scalar multiplication: \(B = 3A\), i.e. \(3A = B\). (The order 2x2 is irrelevant; \(9A = B\) would need each element multiplied by 9.)

working: With \(A^T = A\) and \(B^T = B\): \((AB-BA)^T = (AB)^T-(BA)^T = B^TA^T - A^TB^T = BA - AB = -(AB-BA)\). A matrix equal to the negative of its transpose is skew-symmetric. It need not be null, since AB and BA generally differ.

For an n x n matrix, scaling every entry by k scales the determinant by \(k^n\) (k factors out of each of the n rows). So \(|A| = |kB| = k^n|B|\). Verified numerically for n=3 with k=2.5: \(|kB|/|B| = 15.625 = 2.5^3\).

\(A+B\) defined forces A and B to have the same order, say m x n. \(AB\) defined then forces columns of A = rows of B, i.e. n = m. So both are square matrices of the same order. (C) is a true but incomplete consequence; (B) is the full conclusion.

Left-multiply \(B = -A^{-1}BA\) by A: \(AB = -BA\), i.e. \(AB+BA = 0\). Then \((A+B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2 = A^2 + B^2\). Verified with \(A = \mathrm{diag}(1,-1)\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\), which satisfy the hypothesis: \((A+B)^2 = 2I = A^2+B^2\), and it is not the zero matrix, so (A) is wrong.

working: Equal distances each way, so average speed is the harmonic mean: \(\frac{2\cdot 12\cdot 14}{12+14}=\frac{336}{26}=\frac{168}{13}=12\frac{12}{13}\) km/h. Sanity check with \(d=84\) km: times \(7\) h and \(6\) h, total \(168/13\) km/h — matches, and it lies between 12 and 14 as it must.

subtopic: Triangle Identities — A+B+C=π, Half-Angle, and Double-Angle
working: With \(C=90^\circ\), \(\tan\frac{B}{2}=\frac{\sin B}{1+\cos B}=\frac{b/c}{1+a/c}=\frac{b}{c+a}\); since \(b^2=c^2-a^2=(c-a)(c+a)\), this equals \(\sqrt{\frac{c-a}{c+a}}\). Numeric check on the 3-4-5 triangle (\(a=3,b=4,c=5\)): \(\tan(B/2)=\frac{4/5}{8/5}=\tfrac12\) and \(\sqrt{2/8}=\tfrac12\). Option B is negative under the radical (\(a<c\) always), option C is the reciprocal.

subtopic: Triangle Identities — A+B+C=π, Half-Angle, and Double-Angle
working: By the sine rule, \(\frac{\cos C+\cos A}{c+a}=\frac{2\cos\frac{A+C}{2}\cos\frac{A-C}{2}}{2R\cdot 2\sin\frac{A+C}{2}\cos\frac{A-C}{2}}=\frac{\cot\frac{A+C}{2}}{2R}=\frac{\tan\frac{B}{2}}{2R}\), while \(\frac{1-\cos B}{b}=\frac{1-\cos B}{2R\sin B}=\frac{\tan\frac{B}{2}}{2R}\); hence the expression \(=\frac{1}{b}\). Verified numerically on two triangles: \((3,4,5)\) gives \(\frac{4/5}{8}+\frac{3/5}{4}=\tfrac14=\tfrac1b\), and \((2,3,4)\) gives \(\frac{5/8}{6}+\frac{11/16}{3}=\tfrac13=\tfrac1b\) — both single out \(1/b\) over \(1/a\) and \(1/c\).

The terms are \(\frac85,\frac{12}5,\frac{16}5,\frac{20}5,\frac{24}5,\dots\), i.e. \(t_k=\frac{4(k+1)}5\).
